code.title: Reflection basics

followUps:
typeof(X) is fixed at compile time from a type name, while GetType() asks an object what it really is at run time.

For Animal a = new Dog();, typeof(Animal) is Animal but a.GetType() is Dog. So use typeof when you know the type in source, and GetType for an exact-type check such as a.GetType() == typeof(Dog). GetType on null throws NullReferenceException.

You can, using BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance, but you usually should not.

var m = typeof(Foo).GetMethod("Secret", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance);
object r = m.Invoke(foo, new object[] { 1 });

It bypasses the author's encapsulation, breaks when the private name changes, and fails in partial trust or under trimming. Acceptable cases: tests of legacy code, serializers, and tools. Prefer making the member internal with InternalsVisibleTo, or on .NET 8 use UnsafeAccessor.

code.title: typeof vs GetType vs Type.GetType

followUps:
It returns the open generic type definition, List<>, which has a type parameter that is not filled in.

typeof(List<>) prints as List`1 (the 1 is the number of type parameters), and IsGenericTypeDefinition is true. You cannot create an instance from it. First close it: typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(typeof(int)) gives List<int>. DI containers use this for open generic registrations.

Because GetType() is not called on the Nullable at all: boxing a Nullable<int> that has a value boxes just the int.

GetType() is a non-virtual method of object, so the receiver is boxed first. A Nullable with a value boxes to a plain Int32 object, and a Nullable without a value boxes to null (so GetType would throw). Example: int? n = 5; n.GetType() is System.Int32, while typeof(int?) is Nullable<Int32>.

code.title: Custom attribute read by reflection

followUps:
Pseudo-attributes are keywords that look like attributes in source but are stored as metadata flags, not as CustomAttribute rows.

Examples are [Serializable] (becomes a type flag), [DllImport], [StructLayout], [MethodImpl] and [In]/[Out]. Reflection still shows some through properties like Type.IsSerializable, so GetCustomAttributes may not return them. Use the dedicated property or Attributes flags instead.

Inherited controls whether a derived class or override sees the attribute on its base member, but only when you call the lookup with inherit true.

For classes, Inherited = true means typeof(Derived).GetCustomAttribute<X>() finds the base's attribute. For an overridden method it also finds the attribute on the base virtual method, but MemberInfo.GetCustomAttributes(true) ignores inheritance for properties and events, while the Attribute.GetCustomAttribute overloads honour it. Set Inherited = false when a rule must not leak to subclasses.

code.title: Covariance and contravariance

followUps:
Because IReadOnlyList<T> only hands T out, while IList<T> also takes T in, and variance is only safe when T moves in one direction.

IReadOnlyList has a getter and Count, so a list of Dog can safely act as a list of Animal. IList has Add(T) and a setter, so treating a list of Dog as IList<Animal> would let someone add a Cat. The compiler checks this: declaring out T on IList gives error CS1961.

Java uses use-site variance with wildcards, where C# declares variance once on the interface or delegate.

In Java you write List<? extends Animal> (read only, covariant) or List<? super Dog> (write only, contravariant) at each use, and it works for any generic class. C# writes out T/in T at the declaration, only on interfaces and delegates, and only with reference type arguments. Both languages have covariant arrays that fail at run time (ArrayStoreException vs ArrayTypeMismatchException).

code.title: Generic sum without static abstract (C# 7 witness)

followUps:
All three convert a number between types, and they differ only in what happens when the value does not fit.

Example byte.CreateChecked(300) throws OverflowException; byte.CreateSaturating(300) gives 255 (clamps to the max); byte.CreateTruncating(300) gives 44 (keeps the low 8 bits: 300 mod 256). Use Checked when overflow is a bug, Saturating for clamping such as colours, and Truncating for bit-level work and hashing.

Generic code cannot just write checked(a + b) and get overflow checks unless the type defines a checked operator.

In C# 11 an implementing type declares operator checked + next to operator +. Inside a generic method constrained to IAdditionOperators<T,T,T>, the expression checked(a + b) calls the checked operator, and a plain a + b calls the unchecked one. Built-in int and long implement both, so the same method throws OverflowException or wraps depending on the context.

code.title: Extension method pitfalls

followUps:
The compiler uses normal overload resolution, and the more specific parameter type wins, so the List<T> version is chosen for a List.

For list.Count() with extensions on IEnumerable<T> and List<T> the call is better matched to List<T> (an identity conversion beats an interface conversion). The choice uses the static type: if the variable is declared as IEnumerable<T>, the IEnumerable overload runs even when the object is a List. That is why LINQ checks the run-time type inside (for example ICollection) instead of adding overloads.

They let an extension method change a struct in place, which a normal by-value this would copy.

static void Reset(this ref Counter c) { c.N = 0; }
Counter k = new Counter { N = 5 };
k.Reset();   // k.N is 0 now

Without ref, the method would modify a copy. Rules: ref extensions work only on value types (or generics constrained to struct), and the receiver must be a variable, not a temporary. Also in avoids copying a large readonly struct.

code.title: Operator overloading rules

followUps:
Each operator has a special method name starting with op_, for example op_Addition for +.

The compiler turns operator + into a static method called op_Addition with the specialname flag. Others: op_Equality (==), op_Inequality, op_LessThan, op_Implicit, op_Explicit, op_UnaryNegation. Languages without operator syntax (or reflection) call them by those names, and C# 11 checked forms are op_CheckedAddition.

Lifted operators are the automatic versions for Nullable<T> that the compiler builds from your operator on T.

If you define Money + Money for a struct, then Money? + Money? works too: the result is null if either side is null, otherwise the plain operator runs. Example: int? a = 1, b = null; a + b is null. Comparisons are lifted differently: null == null is true, while < and > with a null side give false.

code.title: Expression tree walked and compiled

followUps:
Build the two bodies with one shared parameter, then combine them with Expression.AndAlso.

var p = Expression.Parameter(typeof(T), "x");
var a = new Swap(p).Visit(e1.Body);   // ExpressionVisitor that replaces e1's parameter
var b = new Swap(p).Visit(e2.Body);
return Expression.Lambda<Func<T,bool>>(Expression.AndAlso(a, b), p);

The visitor swap is required: each lambda has its own parameter object, and mixing them throws ArgumentException. This is how specification and filter builders compose queries that EF can still translate.

It makes Compile() produce a delegate that interprets the tree instead of generating IL.

Interpreting starts faster and works where dynamic code is not allowed (iOS, Native AOT), but each evaluation is slower, often several times, than compiled IL. Compiling the same tree 1 time and calling it a million times is best done with IL; compiling once and calling it twice favours interpreting. Without the flag, a runtime that lacks dynamic code falls back to interpretation automatically.

code.title: Caching and delegates beat raw reflection

followUps:
Because it works with untyped values, so each call does extra checks and creates garbage.

Per call: arguments go into a new object[], value types are boxed (an int allocates about 24 bytes), the runtime checks accessibility and argument types, and the call goes through a slower invoker. A million GetValue calls on an int property can allocate tens of megabytes. A cached typed delegate has none of that, which is why caching and delegates are the first fix.

Anything the trimmer or compiler cannot see being used: code reached only by a string name, and code that must be generated at run time.

Examples: Type.GetType("Name") on a type that was trimmed away, reading all properties of a generic T, Reflection.Emit and dynamic code, and MakeGenericType over value types that were never compiled. Fixes: source generators, [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] annotations, and testing the real published binary.

code.title: Generic constraints in action

followUps:
Because the compiler emits a call to Activator.CreateInstance<T>, which uses reflection to find and run the constructor.

A delegate like Func<T> f = () => new Widget(); compiles to a direct constructor call, so it is a normal fast call with no lookup. If you create millions of objects, pass the Func (or cache a compiled factory) instead of using new(). For a few creations the difference does not matter.

Not directly in C# 10 and older, but yes from C# 11 using static abstract interface members.

Pre-11, you pass a Func or use a witness type. In .NET 7 and later, constrain to the interface that declares it: where T : IParsable<T> and call T.Parse(s, null). int, double, Guid and DateTime already implement it. Your own type implements the interface with a public static Parse method.

Because the compiler re-runs the pipeline on every keystroke, and equatable values let it skip the stages whose input did not change.

An incremental generator caches each step. If step outputs compare equal by value (records, ImmutableArray with a custom comparer), later steps are not re-run. Putting a ISymbol or SyntaxNode in the pipeline compares by reference, so every edit looks like a change and the IDE gets slow. Extract a small record of the needed strings and flags first.

Interceptors are a .NET 8 preview feature where a generator replaces a specific call site with a call to its own generated method.

You mark generated code with [InterceptsLocation(file, line, column)], and the compiler calls it instead of the original method at that place. That lets a generator turn a reflection-based call such as app.MapGet or config.Get<T>() into a trimming-safe version without the caller changing code. They are experimental and tied to exact file positions.

code.title: Mini DI container with cycle detection

followUps:
A captive dependency is a long-lived service that holds on to a shorter-lived one, so the short-lived one lives too long.

Example: a singleton Mailer takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor. The first request's DbContext is kept forever, shared across threads that it was never designed for, and not disposed with its scope. Fix: inject a factory (IServiceScopeFactory) and create a scope per operation, or make the consumer scoped. ValidateScopes catches this in development.

It looks at the constructors of the implementation and picks the one with the most parameters that can all be resolved.

If two constructors have the same number of satisfiable parameters and one is not a superset of the other, it throws an ambiguity error. A constructor whose parameters cannot be resolved is skipped. With [ActivatorUtilitiesConstructor] you can mark one explicitly. Example: ctor(A) and ctor(A, B) with B registered picks ctor(A, B).

Nothing that reflection needs, unless something else references it: unused members are removed to make the binary smaller.

If a type's property is only read through GetProperty("Email"), the trimmer cannot see that use, so the property may be deleted and the call returns null at run time. Annotate the parameter with [DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicProperties)] to keep them, or use [DynamicDependency].

Because AOT compiles all code before running, and MakeGenericType may need code for a type combination that was never compiled.

typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(typeof(MyStruct)) needs machine code specialised for a struct, which a JIT would produce on the fly. For reference type arguments the shared canonical code works, so it is often fine. For value types it can fail at run time with a missing-code error, so use known generic instantiations or a source generator.

code.title: Designing APIs around invariant List<T>

followUps:
Because ICollection<T> has Add and Remove that take a T, and variance is only valid when T is used in one direction.

IReadOnlyCollection and IReadOnlyList only return T, so out T is safe. ICollection<Dog> used as ICollection<Animal> would accept Add(new Cat()) and put a Cat into a Dog collection. The compiler refuses the declaration with CS1961.

A small one-time check, but the cast can be a type-check slow path, so avoid it in tight loops.

Converting IEnumerable<Dog> to IEnumerable<Animal> costs no allocation and no copy: the same object is used. The extra cost is when the runtime must verify variance in a cast or interface dispatch, which is slower than an exact-type cast (tens of nanoseconds versus a few). Variance never copies elements.

code.title: Attribute lookup cost: cached vs uncached

followUps:
Key the cache by the assembly load context, or hold it in a weak form, so unloading can free the types.

A static Dictionary<Type, Metadata> keeps every Type alive, which stops a collectible AssemblyLoadContext from unloading. Use ConditionalWeakTable<Type, Metadata> (entries die with the key) or store a cache on the plugin and drop it when you unload. Metadata must not reference the plugin's types strongly from outside.

CustomAttributeData reads attribute arguments without creating the attribute object or running its constructor.

CustomAttributeData.GetCustomAttributes(member) returns the constructor and named arguments as plain values. It is safer for tools: no user code runs, and it works with MetadataLoadContext where the attribute's type cannot be loaded or executed. It is not faster for repeated use, so you still cache the result.
